articles.headline: Religare Finvest’s funding warning came first—but the replay cannot forecast
articles.dek: A disclosed-liability signal appeared before Religare Finvest’s default date under a conservative availability proxy. The result is a fraud-masked historical sequence, not causal proof, a market verdict, or a tradable forecast.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. The thesis is narrow: on the supplied record, Religare Finvest’s disclosed-liability lens registered before the available action-zone lens. The evidence clock is the filing publication time when available, otherwise period end plus 60 days. The stakes are equally narrow: confusing that reconstructed sequence with a live market signal, a causal explanation, or a prediction would overstate what the evidence can bear.*

## The record before the event

Religare Finvest is the desk’s answer only in a defined historical sense. Its funding side is the balance-sheet area that registered stress first in this reconstruction. The first funding signal is attached to the period ended 2016-03-31: an index of 44.3, in the watch band, with no recorded flags. No explicit publication clock is supplied for that observation, so the replay applies its stated fallback of period end plus 60 days. The resulting knowledge-time proxy is 2016-05-30.

The recorded default date is 2018-01-18. The construction therefore records a 19-month lead. The PCA record supplies neither a first action-zone entry nor a lead time. That supports a sequence claim, not a stronger one: among the supplied lenses, the disclosed-liability lens moved first.

The case is fraud-masked. That qualification is decisive. The dossier warns that filings later shown to be falsified can make an institution appear compliant to a threshold engine. Public disclosure can be incomplete or distorted; a visible warning does not establish the full mechanism of failure, and an apparently calm threshold does not demonstrate safety. The [Religare Finvest replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/religare-finvest/) is consequently an event reconstruction, while the [failure-radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) is a current roster built from vetted public dossiers.

## What the lenses saw

The funding lens is a filing-period signal. It uses disclosed liability information and can operate only where a liability series exists. In the historical summary, 10 of 15 failed institutions had such disclosures. The funding signal fired first in 4 cases, with a median lead of 38 months. Those figures describe a selected historical disclosure subset. They are not a prospective hit rate and cannot speak for institutions without the relevant series.

The PCA/SAF lens is also filing-based, but it replays public-disclosure versions of the RBI’s own tripwires. Of 15 failed institutions, 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. It measures a different condition from a liability signal. Its apparent ordering against funding cannot establish that one condition caused the other, particularly where fraud may have impaired the reported inputs.

The model derivation is a third category of evidence. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events and 27 institutions; 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. A simpler heuristic reaches 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic reports 0.645 against a 0.65 gate and fails. It remains diagnostic only.

A filing-period signal is an observation placed on an availability convention. A model statistic is a derived property of a limited historical panel. Neither is a market-price signal. The [historical validation file](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation) and [market-evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) preserve that distinction rather than allowing a model result to be presented as observed market confirmation.

## Why the warning mattered

A liability-side warning can matter because funding is a distinct balance-sheet channel. A lender must sustain assets while meeting obligations through its liability structure. Deterioration in disclosed funding conditions may therefore justify investigation before a public action-zone proxy shows a breach. That is a plausible investigative rationale, not a causal result established by this replay.

Religare Finvest fits the ordering but not the proof. Funding registered watch while the supplied PCA record has no first action-zone moment. The useful, limited implication is that a disclosed-liability deterioration can be a reason to inspect the balance sheet earlier than an action-zone lens alone would permit.

Fraud masking limits even that implication. Distorted reporting can delay, suppress or alter the measures being compared. The funding observation is not a calibrated failure probability, a determination of default risk, or a substitute for forensic work. The dossier assigns the problem of falsified filings to the forensic screen rather than claiming that disclosed thresholds can solve it.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. This is one fraud-masked institution reconstructed under **PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT**. The historical evidence is not validated-backtest eligible, not real-money eligible, and lacks a bitemporal input contract. Its availability basis is an explicit publication clock when present and otherwise period end plus 60 days. Lead times are explicitly optimistic. The recorded 19-month advantage may exceed what a fully audited contemporaneous information set would have delivered.

Coverage is also selective. The funding lens only sees institutions disclosing a liability series. Five of the 15 failed institutions in the funding summary lack that observation. Missing data remain missing: they are neither evidence of sound funding nor a measured warning. A finding from the observable subset cannot automatically generalize to the unobserved subset.

The model does not rescue the story. Its temporal gate fails, while the conformal alarm is retained as a diagnostic with historical tier wiring suspended pending prospective revalidation. The strongest conclusion is therefore not that funding screens predict failure. It is that this replay makes liability disclosures a reasonable first place to investigate, while leaving open data availability, fraud masking and construction choices as explanations for the apparent order.

## What today's board shares

Today’s board is not evidence about the historical event. As of 2026-09-22, it contains 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange from a 2025-03-31 filing aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow from 2026-03-31 and aged 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow from 2025-09-30 and aged 12 months.

These are published rules over published components, not failure predictions or credit ratings. The board excludes 21 stale records. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Institutions without vetted public dossiers are absent by design; absence is not a claim of safety.

The market layer is a separate market-price signal, not corroboration for those tiers. It is fresh as of 2026-09-18, but it has no admission, tier or publication authority. Rights and display approval are absent for every expected canonical record, and admitted canonical records are 0/25. Yahoo Finance daily closes, auto-adjusted, cannot validate or alter institution tiers here.

## The next falsifiable test

This thesis should fail if prospective, fresh, vetted public dossiers show that disclosed-liability flags do not precede independently recorded stress more often than other available lenses once an auditable publication clock is applied. It should also fail if a bitemporal dataset removes the apparent lead in fraud-masked cases or shows that the relevant filings were not available when the reconstruction assumes they were known.

Credibility would require the ordering to persist prospectively, with liability-disclosure coverage specified in advance, fraud-masked cases identified separately, missing observations retained as missing, and stale, future-dated or unclocked readings denied signal and tier authority. Until then, this is an investigative hypothesis, not investment advice.

## Follow the pressure chain

Start with the filing-period signal: identify the reporting date, the publication clock and whether a liability series is disclosed. Separate that from an action-zone signal and a forensic concern. Consult a market-price signal only afterward, and only where its use authorities permit it.

LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. [Seiche](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) covers **system dollar-funding capacity**. [Undertow](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) covers **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**. These are distinct research boundaries. A balance-sheet warning can justify checking the other domains; it cannot establish either one.

Seiche’s current editorial read is guarded: its composite is 39.6, EROSION, and its note says modelled or slow-moving structure leads while current market plumbing has not broadly confirmed it. Undertow reports partial coverage across several segments. Neither reading proves an institution-specific squeeze, and neither should be fused with Religare Finvest’s historical filing sequence.

## Sources, method, and limits

This article relies only on the [failure-radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [historical validation file](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), [market-evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), [Religare Finvest replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/religare-finvest/), [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) and [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json). It is a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT diagnostic, not a validated backtest or real-money record. Its availability convention can overstate lead times, fraud masking can make disclosures look compliant, and liability-series coverage is incomplete. Its appropriate use is disciplined investigation of published evidence, not prediction from a single historical replay.

This is not a credit rating.

articles.headline: Global Trust Bank’s replay: an early threshold warning, and the disclosure problem it could not solve
articles.dek: The recorded capital and asset-quality breaches arrived before Global Trust Bank’s default. But this fraud-masked case is stronger as a lesson in the limits of filing-based surveillance than as a claim that a model called the event.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is not current news and is not a forecast. It is a historical replay of Global Trust Bank, whose default date is 2004-07-24. Similar balance-sheet mechanisms do not imply the same outcome elsewhere.*

Global Trust Bank presents a deliberately uncomfortable answer to the question of which balance sheet should feel stress first. Its recorded supervisory-threshold signal appeared in reported capital adequacy and non-performing assets, not in a scoreable funding series and not in a market-price signal. For the period ended 2002-03-31, the replay records CRAR and NNPA breaches, a `threshold_2` action-zone status, and a knowledge-time proxy of 2002-05-30. That is a 25-month lead to default.

The finding matters, but only within its narrow evidential boundary. It is a filing-period signal reconstructed with a publication proxy where an explicit publication clock is unavailable. It is not proof that a tradable market anticipated the event, and it is not a model-derived probability of default. Most importantly, the institution is fraud-masked. The case says both that disclosed deterioration can warrant scrutiny and that reported disclosure can be the wrong object to trust.

## The record before the event

The first recorded action-zone entry was FY2002, for the period ended 2002-03-31. The stated breaches were CRAR and NNPA. The system assigns the knowledge-time proxy of 2002-05-30, then measures the interval to the 2004-07-24 default date as 25 months.

That chronology is not a clean point-in-time record. Historical evidence is labelled `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`. The availability rule uses an explicit publication clock when present; otherwise it assumes period end plus 60 days. There is no bitemporal input contract. The replay is not validated-backtest eligible and is not real-money eligible. Its lead times are explicitly described as optimistic.

A period end is not the same thing as public knowledge. A proxy can make disclosures appear more uniformly available than they were, and can overstate the practical time available to investigate, fund, sell, or hedge. The replay therefore supports an investigative observation: reported capital and reported asset quality entered a defined danger zone before the event. It does not establish an executable historical trade or a contemporaneous credit decision.

The broader PCA summary covers 15 failed institutions, of which 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. That is useful context for a threshold lens, not a universal failure clock. The underlying limitations are available in the [historical validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation) and the institution-specific [Global Trust Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/global-trust-bank/).

## What the lenses saw

The PCA lens saw the first recorded warning: CRAR and NNPA crossed the stated action-zone framework. This is a filing-period signal. It concerns reported loss-absorption capacity and reported impaired assets. The economic logic is straightforward but conditional: worsening impaired assets can require provisions or generate losses; losses can reduce capital; a smaller capital buffer leaves less room for further deterioration.

That logic is balance-sheet arithmetic, not an assertion that every threshold breach ends in default. The dossier does not provide a complete sequence of losses, liabilities, counterparties, withdrawals, or interventions. It cannot establish a complete causal route from the reported period to the later default.

The funding lens did not deliver a competing signal. It is `scoreable: false` for Global Trust Bank, with no first signal and no lead time. This is missing-data information, not a positive finding on funding resilience. The funding lens can only observe institutions that disclose a liability series. No usable signal cannot be translated into stable funding.

Nor does this replay contain a market-price warning. A market-derived reading is conceptually different from a filing signal: it reflects price movement rather than reported balance-sheet information. The historical case offers no scoreable funding lead and no stated market lead. It should not be rewritten as evidence that markets confirmed the threshold breach.

Finally, fraud masking changes the hierarchy of evidence. The validation note states that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can look compliant to any threshold engine; the forensic screen owns those cases. Reported ratios can identify disclosed vulnerability. They cannot independently authenticate the reports from which those ratios are made.

## Why the warning mattered

The warning mattered because it changed the right investigative question. Once reported capital and reported non-performing assets cross a supervisory threshold, the task is no longer simply to ask whether the institution looks healthy. It is to examine how much further asset deterioration the reported capital base can absorb, whether the disclosed asset-quality measure is credible, and what information is missing from the liability side.

This is not a claim that the threshold caused the outcome. It is a claim about triage. A defined breach creates a reason to intensify diligence on capital, assets, funding disclosures, and reporting integrity.

The distinction between a signal and a verdict is essential here. The recorded breach is a filing-period observation. The 25-month lead is a construction-PIT derivation from the selected availability rule and the default date. Neither is equivalent to a verified, real-time warning available on an exact market clock. The value of the replay lies in preserving that distinction rather than erasing it.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any claim that the threshold engine “called” Global Trust Bank. The institution is fraud-masked. A system based on reported CRAR and NNPA can be misled if reports are unreliable. Its historical availability also relies on period end plus 60 days where publication timing is absent, and the dossier says lead times are optimistic.

The aggregate diagnostics add restraint rather than rescue. The hazard panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, with 179 censored or unusable rows excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval of 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic score reaches 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only.

Those figures do not promote construction-PIT work into a validated forecast. The proper conclusion is narrower: the replay records a prior disclosed threshold breach, while simultaneously documenting why reported thresholds alone cannot settle a fraud-masked case.

## What today's board shares

Today’s board is not a continuation of this historical case. As of 2026-09-21, it lists 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, as of 2025-03-31, with an age of 18 months and a score of 74.9. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, as of 2026-03-31, age 6 months, score 77.8. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, as of 2025-09-30, age 12 months, score 66.0.

These are board tiers, not default predictions, credit ratings, or evidence that any named institution resembles Global Trust Bank. The board excludes 21 stale institutions. It presents one row per institution with a fresh vetted public dossier; institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design, not scored from memory.

The current market layer is fresh and knowledge-authorized, but it has no admission, publication, or tier authority: admitted canonical records are 0/25. Market-derived display is not approved for every expected canonical record. Thus current market data cannot authorize board tiers. Read the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) alongside the [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), not as interchangeable evidence.

## The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if prospectively collected, properly time-stamped disclosures show that action-zone capital and asset-quality breaches do not identify subsequent fragility after disclosure integrity is independently examined. It weakens further if exact publication times replace the 60-day proxy and the apparent lead time disappears.

The test is practical: preserve each filing’s exact availability time, validate reported inputs, retain missing liability disclosures as missing rather than benign, and evaluate threshold and forensic lenses prospectively. If that process does not improve on disclosed-ratio heuristics, the claimed early-warning value should be reduced rather than defended by retrospective reconstruction.

## Follow the pressure chain

Begin with asset quality: NNPA points to reported impairment. Move to capital: CRAR points to the reported buffer against losses. Then ask whether liabilities are disclosed well enough for funding analysis; Global Trust Bank shows why no scoreable funding signal is not evidence of strength. Finally, test disclosure integrity, because fraud masking can make apparent ratio comfort unreliable.

LiquiLens addresses **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. It should be paired, not confused, with Seiche’s **system dollar-funding capacity** view and Undertow’s **market liquidity and executable exit capacity** view. These are different questions: a lender’s reported resilience, the capacity of dollar-funding plumbing, and the ability to exit a position need not move together. See [Seiche’s overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) and [Undertow’s board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json).

## Sources, method, and limits

The relevant primary materials are the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [historical validation](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), [market evidence](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), and the [Global Trust Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/global-trust-bank/). Broader context is collected in [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/) and [LiquiLens investigations](https://liquilens.in/investigations/).

The historical record remains construction-PIT, not fully point-in-time. Its 60-day filing proxy applies where explicit publication clocks are absent; lead times are optimistic; it is neither validated-backtest eligible nor real-money eligible. Missing liability disclosures constrain the funding lens. Fraud masking constrains every interpretation based on reported thresholds. The current board is a diagnostic screen, not investment advice, a credit rating, or a forecast of failure.

This is not a credit rating.

articles.headline: Altico’s historical warning was funding dependence, not a forecast of failure
articles.dek: A construction-period replay identifies commercial-paper reliance as Altico’s earliest documented vulnerability. That is a filing-period signal about rollover exposure, not proof that markets priced distress or that a model forecast default.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Altico before its 2019-09-12 default. The key filing period ended 2017-03-31; the conservative knowledge-time proxy is 2017-05-30. The market-layer date is 2026-09-18 and publication is 2026-09-20.*

The proposition is deliberately narrow: Altico’s balance sheet should have been investigated first through funding, because disclosed commercial-paper reliance created rollover-freeze exposure. That is neither a claim that the flag proved distress nor that it forecast a default. It distinguishes a filing-period signal from a market-price signal and from a model derivation. The former records a disclosed liability structure; the second would show repricing by market participants; the third converts inputs into a score or rule. None is interchangeable.

## The record before the event

Altico was an NBFC, its funding lens was scoreable, and the dossier records no fraud-masking designation. Its first funding signal was a 23.7 index reading in the stable band at the 2017-03-31 period end. The accompanying flag was explicit: **“CP reliance 29% (rollover-freeze exposure)”**. The replay assigns a 27-month lead to the 2019-09-12 default.

That interval must not be mistaken for a tradable warning. The evidence status is `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, the construction uses period end plus 60 days. The dossier says lead times are optimistic, the record has no bitemporal input contract, and it is neither validated-backtest eligible nor real-money eligible. A period-end observation is therefore not proof that an outside creditor, investor, or counterparty possessed it on that date.

Readers can inspect the [Altico replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/altico/) alongside the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) and [validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation). The appropriate conclusion is that the liability structure merited investigation, not that the historical timestamp established actionable foresight.

## What the lenses saw

The funding lens saw a disclosed dependency on CP and labelled its relevant vulnerability: a possible rollover freeze. It did not document an actual freeze, identify the cause of the later default, or establish a complete causal chain. Its contribution was more limited: it isolated a liability channel through which refinancing conditions could become consequential while the asset side remained outstanding.

The historical funding record is small and selectively observable. Of 15 failed institutions, 10 had liability disclosures, and the funding signal fired first for 4; median lead was 38 months. The lens can only assess institutions that disclose a liability series. Missing disclosure is missing data, not evidence of comfortable funding. Nor does a funding flag tell readers whether another lens supplied an earlier or more useful warning.

The broader model diagnostics reinforce restraint. The hazard panel had 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows were excluded. Its leave-one-institution-out AUC was 0.752, with an interval of 0.338 to 1.0. The temporal result was 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and remains diagnostic only. On the same held-out rows, the heuristic AUC was 0.799. These figures describe model derivations under constrained historical construction; they do not validate a live failure forecast.

## Why the warning mattered

A liability requiring renewal can create pressure before a broad balance-sheet screen visibly changes. If renewal becomes less available or more costly, replacement liquidity becomes the immediate question. That mechanism explains why CP reliance is a sensible diligence prompt. It does not assert an unrecorded Altico event.

The stable band is central to the interpretation. A stable composite reading did not erase the documented funding flag; equally, the flag did not overrule the stable reading and pronounce distress. The useful lesson is about sequencing: an individual funding dependency can deserve scrutiny before a composite level settles the broader case.

A separate public-disclosure replay of RBI PCA or SAF tripwires found that 5 of 15 failed institutions entered an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. That does not make the regulatory lens superior to the funding lens, or vice versa. Filings later shown falsified can look compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that limitation.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat an overconfident thesis. CP reliance of 29% may have been a visible financing choice rather than evidence of imminent impairment. The funding index was 23.7 and stable. The 27-month historical interval is long enough for an institution’s funding mix, liquidity, and counterparties to change materially. Because the availability clock is partly proxied, the replay cannot prove the precise contemporaneous information set.

The sample further limits any generalisation. Only 10 of 15 failed institutions disclosed usable liabilities, and only 4 had the funding signal fire first. The temporal model missed its stated gate; the heuristic outperformed the hazard measure on the reported held-out rows. Nothing here shows that CP reliance outperformed every alternative warning method, or that it distinguished Altico from every comparable lender.

The defensible thesis is therefore conditional: the disclosure made Altico a stronger candidate for rollover-capacity diligence. It did not show failure was inevitable, determine timing, or provide a complete explanation of the default.

## What today's board shares

Today’s board is not an Altico replay. As of 2026-09-20, it reports 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions, with 21 excluded as stale. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange with a 2025-03-31 as-of date and age of 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 2026-03-31 and 6 months; ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow at 2025-09-30 and 12 months.

These are published screens, not ratings or predictions. The rule can assign yellow for a funding flag among other conditions. But the market layer lacks tier authority: records are fresh and clocked, yet display and tier use are not approved for every expected canonical record. Its [market evidence interface](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) identifies Yahoo Finance daily closes as source, but the dossier does not permit market-derived display to support a published tier conclusion.

## The next falsifiable test

This account would weaken if a prospective dataset, timed to actual publication, found that disclosed CP reliance did not precede measurable funding stress more often than comparable balance-sheet indicators after controlling for disclosure availability. It would weaken further if flagged institutions repeatedly renewed funding without observable pressure while other usable lenses consistently gave earlier warnings.

The test must retain actual availability times and preserve absent liability disclosure as missing rather than benign. It should compare the funding signal with independently observed subsequent stress outcomes. Until then, this construction-period replay is a hypothesis generator, not a validated trading rule, default model, or substitute for institution-specific diligence.

## Follow the pressure chain

The products have distinct remits. LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**: funding mix, disclosure quality, and lender-specific pressure points. Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**; its [overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) offers system context. Undertow covers **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**; its [board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) reports incomplete segment coverage rather than a universal all-clear.

A system-funding divergence is a warning to investigate, not proof of a squeeze. A lender funding flag does not prove an exit problem, and partial market coverage cannot be read as normality. The diagnostic handoff is to locate pressure: institutional liabilities, system funding capacity, or executable exit capacity.

## Sources, method, and limits

Core materials are the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [historical validation](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), [market evidence](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), and [Altico replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/altico/). Further desk material appears in [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/) and [investigations](https://liquilens.in/investigations/).

The limits are substantive: filing-availability-proxied construction, a 60-day fallback lag, optimistic lead times, no bitemporal contract, selective liability disclosures, and no inference of calm from missing data. The replay identifies a historical balance-sheet mechanism worth testing. It does not convert that mechanism into a repeatable forecast.

This is not a credit rating. Research and market data, not investment advice.

articles.headline: Before the event: what Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank's filings did and did not reveal
articles.dek: A construction-PIT replay of Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank: the first published regulatory or funding signal, the disclosure clock, the miss, and the boundary that survives into today's screen.
articles.body_markdown:
Nothing in today's Failure Radar evidence cleared the bar for a fresh institution story. This is therefore a historical replay, **not current news and not a forecast**. It opens the public Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank record because a quiet daily tape is better used to examine what an early-warning system could actually have known than to manufacture a new alarm.

The recorded outcome date is **2023-11-24**. LiquiLens's reconstruction asks two narrower questions. Did the disclosed ratios enter a published regulatory action zone? Did the disclosed liability structure enter a funding-fragility band? It does not ask whether a modern model, armed with later revisions and hindsight, can draw a persuasive line through the event.

## The record before the event

The first regulatory action-zone row is dated **2021-03-31**, with a conservative knowledge-time proxy of **2021-05-30**. Its status is **saf_triggered**, its breached fields are **NNPA**, and its recorded lead is **29 months**.

The funding replay is independently scoreable: **True**. Its first signal is dated **not observed**, with knowledge-time proxy **not available**, index **unavailable**, band **not observed**, flags **none published**, and lead **unavailable months**.

Those two rows are allowed to disagree. Regulatory thresholds look for capital and asset-quality boundaries. Funding fragility looks for liability dependence and rollover exposure. One can fire while the other stays silent because they describe different failure physics.

## What the lenses saw

The [public replay page](https://liquilens.in/replay/abhyudaya-co-operative-bank/) preserves the observed entries and misses side by side. The regulatory lens reports the institution against the framework's own tripwires. The funding lens requires liability disclosures and abstains when a usable series is absent. The hazard model excludes fraud-masked failures from fitting because fabricated disclosures carry no honest deterioration signal.

Across the full India record, the regulatory replay summary contains **15** failed institutions and **5** first action-zone entries, with a median recorded lead of **41 months**. The funding replay contains **10** institutions with liability disclosures and **4** first funding signals.

Those are diagnostic counts, not a validated backtest. The dossiers use explicit publication time when it exists and otherwise a conservative period-end-plus-filing-lag proxy. The source record says that the missing complete revision archive can make reconstructed lead times optimistic.

## Why the warning mattered

An early warning matters only if it names a mechanism and leaves time to test it. An action-zone breach says capital or asset quality crossed a supervisory boundary. A funding flag says the liability structure may be exposed to rollover or withdrawal. Neither statement proves the eventual outcome; both can tell a risk team what evidence to demand next.

For Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank, the useful question is which lens spoke first and which stayed silent. The answer above is more valuable than a blended retrospective score because it preserves responsibility. A ratio model should not take credit for a funding signal, and a funding model should not claim to have seen fabricated assets.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case is the historical construction itself. A period-end metric is not necessarily what a decision-maker saw on that date. Later amendments may overwrite the original. A fixed filing-lag proxy is conservative about immediate availability but cannot reconstruct every revision. That makes this a mechanism diagnostic, not proof of live foresight.

The record's fraud-masked flag for this case is ****. If true, honest-looking published ratios can be a false negative for any disclosure-based engine. If false, the absence of a signal can still be a real miss. LiquiLens keeps both categories visible because removing them would turn research into marketing.

## What today's board shares

Today's board contains **0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow and 15 green** rows. That is not evidence that any current institution is “the next Abhyudaya Co-operative Bank.” No similarity model is asserted here. The legitimate connection is methodological: current filings, market prices, regulatory distance and funding coverage still arrive on different clocks and can still disagree.

The board also excludes **21** stale dossiers from current presentation. That abstention is part of the signal. An institution missing from the current table is not thereby safe; it may simply lack a fresh vetted record.

## The next falsifiable test

For a current name, record the filing period, knowledge-time proxy and market date before reading the tier. Then ask whether a newer filing confirms the same asset-quality, capital or funding direction. If it reverses, the old screen should fall. If a dark funding lens becomes observable, grade whether it confirms or contradicts the tier. If the model cannot state what would change its mind, the historical lesson has not been learned.

## Follow the pressure chain

articles.headline: First Leasing replay draws the line between disclosed stress and forensic risk
articles.dek: First Leasing Company Of India’s fraud-masked default produced no recorded first action-zone or funding signal in this construction replay. That is a limit on reported-balance-sheet surveillance, not evidence of calm.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. The default examined here occurred on 2013-12-02. It is not investment advice and not a credit rating.*

Which institution balance sheet should feel financial stress first, and why? First Leasing Company Of India supplies an uncomfortable answer: sometimes a screen built from public disclosures cannot establish that it did.

The case is an NBFC recorded as fraud-masked. Its PCA-style record contains no recorded first action-zone entry or lead time. Its funding record is scoreable, but contains no recorded first funding signal or lead time. Those absences do not show that reported capital, asset quality, or funding conditions were sound. They show that this replay did not document a qualifying disclosed threshold signal before default.

That distinction is the point of the case. A filing-period signal arises from reported information becoming available under the replay’s publication-clock rule. A market-price signal comes from market data, with separate authority and display constraints. A model derivation can arrange available inputs, but cannot make missing or falsified disclosures reliable. First Leasing is therefore a boundary test, not an early-warning victory.

## The record before the event

First Leasing Company Of India is identified as fraud-masked, with default dated 2013-12-02. The PCA lens records neither a first action-zone date nor lead months. The funding lens is scoreable, yet records neither a first signal nor lead months. In this construction, those are missing findings, not affirmative resilience findings.

The historical evidence is labelled `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`. It is not eligible as a validated backtest or a real-money test, and it does not have a bitemporal input contract. Where an explicit publication clock is unavailable, information availability is proxied as period end plus 60 days. The dossier says resulting lead times are optimistic. The [historical validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation) should therefore be read as a public-disclosure replay using a conservative timing proxy, rather than proof of a participant’s real-time information set.

The narrow proposition is that disclosed deterioration can register in an action-zone, deterioration, or funding lens before a failure. But threshold engines only receive reported disclosure. If filings were later shown falsified, apparent compliance may describe the inputs rather than the institution’s condition.

## What the lenses saw

Across the failed-institution record, the PCA-style lens entered an action zone first for 5 of 15 failed institutions, with median lead of 41 months. The funding lens had liability disclosures for 10 of 15 failed institutions, fired first for 4, and had median lead of 38 months. These are summaries of disclosed historical cases. They do not establish that either lens covers every failure route.

First Leasing supplies no such sequence. The fraud-masked designation controls the interpretation. The validation note says institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine, while the forensic screen owns those cases. That is a stated limitation. It is not grounds to reconstruct an unobserved warning from evidence outside this dossier.

The India diagnostic covers 48 institutions across two decades and reports 88.9% of non-fraud failures flagged, with median lead of 21.5 months. But it has the same filing-availability-proxied construction and optimistic-lead limitation. The [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) identifies it as a construction-PIT diagnostic, not prospective validation.

## Why the warning mattered

A useful warning identifies a pressure channel that can be inspected. An action-zone or deterioration signal concerns disclosed balance-sheet conditions. A funding flag concerns disclosed liability information. A forensic indicator concerns whether the disclosed information can be trusted.

First Leasing shows why those categories cannot be merged. The absence of recorded PCA and funding leads does not exonerate the institution. Conversely, the fraud-masked label does not establish a concealed capital path or liability sequence; the dossier provides neither. What it does establish is an evidentiary handoff. Reported thresholds assess reported conditions. Questions about disclosure integrity require forensic work.

Model diagnostics require the same restraint. The leave-one-institution-out hazard AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic AUC is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal diagnostic AUC is 0.645, below the 0.65 gate, and is diagnostic only. Construction-PIT diagnostics cannot promote. These measures can frame questions; they cannot turn this replay into a calibrated failure forecast.

## The strongest counter-case

The counter-case can defeat the thesis. If fraud-masked failures sit outside threshold surveillance whenever the thresholds miss them, the framework may be weakest precisely where users need protection most. A system that cannot distinguish truly reassuring reported disclosures from false reassurance has a material blind spot.

This case supports that criticism. The dossier does not show that fraud masking caused the default. It does not identify a hidden funding sequence. It does not establish that forensic review would have produced an earlier public warning. Calling this a forensic handoff honestly describes the boundary, but does not prove that the handoff succeeds.

The narrower defence is not that the framework caught First Leasing. It did not document a qualifying filing-based lead. The defence is that relabelling the missing findings as stability would be worse. The framework preserves both the missing findings and the fraud-masked designation. Its useful claim is limited to a division of labour: disclosure-driven lenses can surface disclosure-driven pressure, but cannot authenticate every disclosure.

## What today's board shares

Today’s board is not a replay result for First Leasing and must not inherit its outcome. As of 2026-09-14, it shows 0 red, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green institutions; 21 stale cases are excluded. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with filings as of 2025-03-31 and an age of 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow, with filings as of 2026-03-31 and an age of 6 months. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow, with filings as of 2025-09-30 and an age of 12 months.

Their displayed signal lists are empty, and their market drawdown fields are not recorded. The [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board) is consequently a filing-based comparison view, not a First Leasing analogue.

The market layer is available as of 2026-09-11 and was retrieved on 2026-09-14. Yet market-derived display, model, tier, and publication use are not approved for every expected canonical record. Admitted canonical records are 0/25, and the layer has no tier authority. A market-price signal must not be inserted into a filing-period tier merely because prices were retrieved.

## The next falsifiable test

The proposed division of labour is testable. Future fresh vetted public dossiers should preserve explicit publication time when present and otherwise retain the period-end-plus-60-days proxy. Before outcomes are known, the record can test whether action-zone, deterioration, or funding signals precede usable forensic findings, and whether public inconsistencies in fraud-masked cases can be identified before default.

The thesis fails if a properly time-stamped prospective record finds that filing-based thresholds do not lead useful investigative evidence. It also fails if purported forensic findings do not survive review, or if missing disclosed signals are repeatedly treated as comfort despite later contrary evidence. Until that record exists, historical leads remain optimistic construction-PIT diagnostics.

## Follow the pressure chain

Begin with the reported balance sheet: is a qualifying action-zone, deterioration, or funding condition actually disclosed? Then ask whether the observation is fresh and eligible under the published rule. Finally ask whether the disclosure deserves trust. First Leasing warns against skipping that final question.

The product boundaries are explicit. Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity**. LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. Undertow covers **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**. The [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview) and [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json) can add system or exit context, but neither supplies a missing forensic fact for this institution replay.

For the underlying case record, see the [First Leasing replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/first-leasing-company-of-india/). The appropriate response is investigation of the pressure chain, not a mechanical verdict from a colour label.

## Sources, method, and limits

Primary dossier outputs are the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [historical validation](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), and [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets). Related material is available through the [LiquiLens replay archive](https://liquilens.in/replay/) and [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/).

The method presents one row per institution with a fresh vetted public dossier. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design, and nothing is scored from memory. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings may remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. The conformal alarm remains a diagnostic, while its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation.

First Leasing is useful because it refuses false resolution. It records no documented filing-based threshold lead, preserves the fraud-masked limitation, separates filing authority from market authority, and leaves the forensic question open where the evidence remains open.

articles.headline: Madhavpura’s replay shows where a balance-sheet radar can go blind
articles.dek: Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank produced no recorded conventional early funding or action-zone warning. Fraud masking means that silence cannot be treated as resilience: a disclosure-driven screen cannot verify a balance sheet when reported evidence may be false.

A filing-period signal, a market-price signal, and a model derivation are different objects. A filing-period signal describes what a dated public disclosure permits a screen to observe. A market-price signal is a repricing observation only when its inputs are authorized for that use. A model derivation turns specified inputs into a score or tier; it cannot repair falsified or missing inputs. Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank is classified as a UCB. The historical record gives its default date as 2012-06-04 and explicitly marks the case fraud-masked. A benign-looking ratio would then be a property of the reported input, not a verified property of the balance sheet.

Historical evidence uses an explicit publication clock when present and otherwise a period-end plus 60-days proxy. It lacks a bitemporal input contract, is not validated-backtest eligible, is not real-money eligible, and its lead times are optimistic.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case defeats an overextended thesis. The replay is too sparse to establish that Madhavpura’s balance sheet visibly deteriorated in a particular sequence before default. Neither conventional lens records a first signal, and the dossier supplies no line-item chronology from which to reconstruct one. “Unknown” is more defensible than a claim that hidden stress was demonstrably present at a specific earlier point.

Fraud masking explains why silence cannot be reassurance; it does not prove that a public balance-sheet screen could have identified fraud earlier. The counter-case should prevail unless independently auditable forensic evidence supplies that missing bridge.

Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design; nothing is scored from memory. The conformal alarm is diagnostic only, with historical tier wiring suspended and no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Those rules stop a plausible narrative from becoming unsupported evidence.

Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange on a 2025-03-31 filing aged 18 months. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow on a 2026-03-31 filing aged 6 months. articles.dek: The historical replay records a watch-band funding signal before Religare Finvest’s default. That makes disclosed liabilities an early pressure channel to investigate, not a causal explanation or a forecast.

Global Trust Bank is the narrow answer to the desk question only in one specific sense: its disclosed capital and asset-quality measures entered the first recorded RBI action zone before the event. The replay records threshold_2 breaches in CRAR and NNPA. That is a filing-period signal: reported balance-sheet weakness at a stated reporting date, made usable at a stated or proxied knowledge time. It is not a market-price signal, because no authorised market reading is used to establish this historical conclusion. And it is not a model derivation masquerading as an observed fact: the lead time follows a construction rule and carries explicit timing limits.

The thesis is therefore modest. On the public record represented here, Global Trust Bank’s first observable fault line was loss-absorption capacity exposed to impaired assets, rather than a disclosed funding alarm. ## The record before the event

The first PCA action-zone entry is recorded at the period ending 2002-03-31, labelled FY2002. The first-action-zone record identifies CRAR and NNPA breaches, and gives 2002-05-30 as the knowledge-time proxy. The default date is 2004-07-24; the stated lead is 25 months.

The default date tells us when the subsequent event occurred. The replay uses an explicit publication clock when one is present and otherwise applies period end plus 60 days. That convention is a modelled availability rule, not proof of what every investor, creditor or supervisor knew on a particular day.

Global Trust Bank is fraud-masked. That disclosure is central rather than decorative: filings later shown falsified can look compliant to any threshold engine, while a reported breach may also understate or misdate real weakness. The full case record is available on the [Global Trust Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/global-trust-bank/).

The PCA lens replays public-disclosure versions of RBI action-zone tripwires. In the historical PCA summary, 5 of 15 failed institutions entered an action zone first, with median lead of 41 months. The funding lens cannot confirm or contest that sequence for this bank. Global Trust Bank’s funding series was not scoreable; it has no first funding signal and no funding lead time. Among the failed-institution summary, liability disclosures existed for 10 of 15 institutions, the funding signal fired first for 4, and median lead was 38 months. Global Trust Bank is outside that scoreable group.

Missing funding data are an unknown, not a clean bill of health. The lens only sees institutions that disclose a liability series. It cannot infer durable deposits, stable refinancing or the absence of a concealed run-risk where that disclosure is unavailable.

CRAR and NNPA point to a plausible balance-sheet pressure chain. A capital-adequacy breach indicates less buffer against risk-weighted exposures. It may flag disclosed deterioration, but it cannot certify the absence of worse deterioration, establish the true timing of losses, or distinguish a reliable report from a misleading one.

Third, no scoreable funding sequence exists for Global Trust Bank. Without it, the proposed progression from impaired assets to capital compression to creditor or depositor sensitivity remains a plausible chain, not a demonstrated chain. The counter-case is not that the PCA record is irrelevant; it is that this evidence cannot prove that public ratios alone would have produced a dependable supervisory verdict, investment decision or generalisable prediction.

The correct use is an alert for investigation. It is not evidence that every CRAR-and-NNPA breach ends in default, and it is not evidence that institutions without a funding flag are safe.

## What today's board shares

The [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) does not authorise market-derived display or tier use for every expected canonical record. A fresh market pack is therefore not interchangeable with a permitted market-price signal.

LiquiLens covers **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**. Seiche covers **system dollar-funding capacity** through its [overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview). ## The next falsifiable test

The thesis weakens if authentic, time-stamped pre-event disclosures show that Global Trust Bank had not breached the relevant CRAR and NNPA action-zone conditions by the stated knowledge time, or show that the recorded breach derives solely from later reconstruction rather than then-available information.

It strengthens if independently time-stamped liability disclosures show subsequent funding pressure consistent with the proposed chain. Either test must preserve original publication timing and identify falsified filings. Otherwise, apparent lead time remains potentially optimistic.

## Follow the pressure chain

Start with impaired assets and reported loss recognition. Ask whether those pressures compress capital. Then ask whether a reduced buffer affects confidence and whether liability pressure is independently observable. Do not reverse the sequence merely because funding distress is easier to narrate after a failure.

For current work, require fresh vetted public dossiers, remove stale, future-dated and unclocked readings from signal or tier authority, and treat absent liability disclosure as unknown. **Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing here is scored from memory.**

## The record before the event

Altico defaulted on 2019-09-12. Its recorded first funding signal belongs to the period ending 2017-03-31, with 2017-05-30 used as the knowledge-time proxy. The recorded lead was 27 months. articles.headline: Nedungadi Bank’s first recorded pressure point was capital, not a market call
articles.dek: The historical replay identifies a CRAR action-zone breach before Nedungadi Bank’s default, but its timing is a filing-availability proxy and its evidence cannot support a forecast, a credit verdict, or a claim of causation.
articles.body_markdown:
*This is a historical replay, not current news and not a forecast. It examines Nedungadi Bank through a filing-availability-proxied construction-PIT record. The default date is 2002-11-02; the first action-zone period-end is 1999-03-31, with a knowledge-time proxy of 1999-05-30. Similar mechanisms do not imply the same outcome at another institution.*

The narrow answer to the desk question is Nedungadi Bank’s disclosed capital position. The first recorded qualifying signal was a CRAR breach in the RBI action zone, attached to FY1999. That is a filing-period signal: a reconstruction of when a disclosed condition could have become available under the dossier’s publication convention. It is not a market-price signal, because no market-derived measure establishes the case. Nor is it a model derivation that can convert the breach into a failure probability.

The distinction is decisive. The replay measures a lead of 41 months from its availability proxy to the recorded default. It does not show that every relevant observer possessed, interpreted, or acted on the information at that time. It does not prove that the capital breach caused the default. It says only that, among the available lenses, capital was the first recorded action-zone pressure point.

## The record before the event

Nedungadi Bank entered the first RBI PCA/SAF action zone at the 1999-03-31 period-end, designated FY1999, because of CRAR. Where no explicit publication clock is present, the record uses period-end plus 60 days. That yields the 1999-05-30 knowledge-time proxy. The institution’s default is recorded on 2002-11-02.

This is explicitly labelled `PERIOD_END_PROXY_CONSTRUCTION_PIT`. It is not eligible for validated backtesting or real-money use; it has no bitemporal input contract; and the dossier says its lead times are optimistic. A reporting date, a proxy availability date, and the moment at which a depositor, investor, supervisor, or counterparty understands a filing are different events. The 41-month interval must therefore be read as a construction result, not as a contemporaneous trading or supervisory record.

The case file is available in the [Nedungadi Bank replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/nedungadi-bank/). The wider rule set and roster are on the [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board). Neither source makes the historical replay a present-tense finding.

Nedungadi carries no fraud-masked flag. That is not a general assurance about disclosure quality. The validation record warns that institutions whose filings were later shown falsified can appear compliant to a threshold engine; the forensic screen owns that failure mode. Missing, unusable, or misleading disclosure is not evidence of calm.

## What the lenses saw

The PCA lens recorded CRAR as Nedungadi’s first action-zone breach. The funding lens was not scoreable: it has no first signal and no lead time for this institution. That absence is a missing-data disclosure, not a favorable funding conclusion. The funding lens can only observe institutions that disclose a liability series.

The historical summaries illustrate why the two lenses should not be collapsed into one story. Of 15 failed institutions, 5 entered an action zone first, with a median lead of 41 months. Of the same 15 failures, 10 had liability disclosures; the funding signal fired first for 4, with a median lead of 38 months. Those figures show that funding and action-zone signals can arrive separately. They do not establish that one lens universally leads the other, and they cannot resolve Nedungadi’s funding condition without the missing liability series.

The hazard work is also diagnostic rather than promotable evidence. Its leave-one-institution-out row AUC is 0.752, with a confidence interval from 0.338 to 1.0. The heuristic score is 0.799 on the same held-out rows. The temporal test AUC is 0.645, below its 0.65 gate. The panel contains 205 rows, 9 events, and 27 institutions, while 179 censored or unusable rows are excluded. The [historical validation record](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation) is a limit disclosure, not a performance certificate.

## Why the warning mattered

An RBI action-zone breach matters because it identifies a regulatory threshold tied, in this case, to capital. The defensible inference is not that the threshold supplied a default clock. It is that a breach can identify a balance-sheet constraint before a recorded failure, and that this constraint deserves investigation alongside asset quality, earnings, funding, management response, and disclosure reliability.

For Nedungadi, the warning mattered because it was concrete and independently specified: CRAR, not an after-the-event composite score and not a price-based alarm. The record supports a pressure-chain hypothesis in which constrained loss-absorption capacity may make adverse developments harder to accommodate. But the dossier does not supply the intervening causal history needed to prove that sequence. It provides no scoreable funding confirmation and no market-price evidence for the institution.

That restraint is the point. A filing-period breach can be useful without being a forecast. A market-price signal would instead describe repricing in traded prices; none is established here. A model output would be a derivation from its inputs and assumptions; it cannot repair unavailable funding evidence or turn proxy timing into observed knowledge.

## The strongest counter-case

The strongest counter-case can defeat any inflated version of the thesis. A capital threshold breach can be an early, noisy regulatory classification rather than a reliable marker of eventual failure. A lender may restore capital, reduce risk, improve earnings, obtain support, or otherwise leave the pressure zone. The 41-month lead leaves substantial room for paths other than default.

The construction itself could overstate the apparent advance warning. The 60-day filing convention is a proxy when an explicit publication clock is absent. The dossier says lead times are optimistic and denies validated-backtest and real-money eligibility. Its temporal diagnostic does not clear its stated gate. Its PCA summary is a public-disclosure replay of RBI tripwires, not a causal account of each institution’s failure.

The missing funding series is equally damaging to an overconfident thesis. The record cannot demonstrate a deposit or wholesale-funding event for Nedungadi, cannot rank capital against funding for this case, and cannot establish that capital was the only important vulnerability. The correct conclusion remains narrower: CRAR was the first recorded qualifying lens, not the sole explanation.

## What today's board shares

The current board is separate from the Nedungadi replay. As of 2026-09-03, it shows 0 red institutions, 1 orange, 3 yellow, and 15 green. Utkarsh Small Finance Bank is orange, with a score of 74.9 and an as-of date of 2025-03-31. Belstar Microfinance Limited is yellow at 77.8, as of 2026-03-31. ESAF Small Finance Bank is yellow at 66.0, as of 2025-09-30.

Those tiers are screens over published components, not credit ratings or failure predictions. The board excludes 21 stale institutions. Institutions without vetted dossiers are absent by design: nothing here is scored from memory. Nothing older than 24 months is presented as current.

The market layer was retrieved on 2026-09-03 but has no publication, admission, signal, or tier authority. Rights and display approvals are not in place for every expected canonical record. The [market evidence index](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets) therefore cannot supply a market confirmation for the board or for the Nedungadi replay.

## The next falsifiable test

The capital-first interpretation would weaken if prospectively timestamped disclosures showed that the CRAR breach was not available by the assumed proxy date. It would weaken further if comparable action-zone breaches regularly resolved without subsequent deterioration, while institutions without such breaches displayed equal or greater recorded distress.

A stronger test requires actual publication clocks, preserved amended-file vintages, distinct capital and liability series, and outcomes observed without retrofitting the rule. Until then, the 41-month figure is an investigative clue. It is not a calibrated probability, a trade signal, or investment advice.

## Follow the pressure chain

For historical institution work, begin with the [LiquiLens replay archive](https://liquilens.in/replay/) and [LiquiLens research](https://liquilens.in/research/). LiquiLens concerns **institution and lender balance-sheet risk**; it is the appropriate lens for a disclosed capital breach and for gaps in institution-level evidence.

The products should not be merged into a single stress verdict. Seiche addresses **system dollar-funding capacity**, as described in the [Seiche overview](https://api.seiche.info/api/overview). Undertow addresses **market liquidity and executable exit capacity**, as described in the [Undertow board](https://api.seiche.info/undertow/board.json). Their different coverage, clocks, and authority gates prevent any of them from substituting for Nedungadi’s unavailable funding evidence.

## Sources, method, and limits

This article uses only the supplied [Failure Radar board](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/board), [historical validation](https://api.liquilens.in/api/failure-radar/validation), [market evidence](https://api.liquilens.in/api/evidence/markets), and [Nedungadi replay](https://liquilens.in/replay/nedungadi-bank/). Historical components were replayed independently on a 48-institution construction-PIT record and fused only for presentation.

The conformal alarm remains diagnostic; its historical tier wiring is suspended and it has no score or tier authority pending prospective revalidation. Where present in the broader framework, Merton PD is a market repricing signal, not a calibrated failure frequency. Stale, future-dated, or unclocked market readings may remain visible but have no signal or tier authority. These limits are not footnotes to the conclusion; they define what the conclusion can mean.
